standard.title: Nominalisation
standard.description: understand the effect of nominalisation in texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can understand how word choice constructs meaning and how different grammatical categories function (AC9E7LA05, AC9E7LA08). They have not yet examined nominalisation — the process of converting verbs and other word classes into nouns — and its effect on tone, abstraction and register.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how nominalisation works and what effects it creates in texts, including changes to tone, abstraction and formality.

nodes.label: What nominalisation is
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify nominalisations in texts and explain the grammatical transformation involved (verb or adjective converted to noun).
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two nominalisations in a provided informative text and name the original verb or adjective form each has been derived from.
nodes.typical_width: Identify nominalisations across a range of informative texts, explaining the grammatical process and comparing the nominalised form with its verbal equivalent in terms of grammatical role in the sentence.
wider: Investigate how nominalisation density varies across text types — compare a newspaper report, an academic article and an informal blog on the same topic
Identify nominalisations in a First Nations or multicultural community text and consider how nominalisation conventions may differ across language backgrounds
Examine how government or bureaucratic documents use nominalisation to create abstract, impersonal official language

response_modes.reason: Identifying nominalisations requires students to work backwards from noun form to verbal origin — a grammatical analysis move that is not obvious. Without explicit attention to the transformation (verb → noun), students may simply note 'formal words' without understanding the grammatical mechanism, which limits the tone analysis at Node 2.

success_criteria: Identifies a nominalised noun in a text and names the verb or adjective it was derived from.
Explains what grammatical role the nominalised form plays in the sentence (subject, object, etc.).

nodes.label: Effect of nominalisation on tone and register
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how nominalisation affects the tone and register of a text — creating abstraction, formality and impersonality — and can discuss the impact of nominalisation on content and potential audiences.
nodes.minimum_width: Nominalise the verbs in two or three sentences and explain how the change in tone (more formal/abstract) could affect how the text is perceived by a reader.
nodes.typical_width: Examine how nominalisation in a range of informative texts creates a formal, abstract or impersonal tone; explain how this affects the content and the relationship constructed with the audience; discuss where nominalisation is appropriate vs where it may obscure meaning.
wider: Rewrite a formal passage using verbal rather than nominalised forms and analyse how this changes the perceived formality, agency and accessibility of the text

Investigate how critical reading of nominalisation can reveal hidden agency — nominalisation often removes the actor from a sentence, which can have ideological effects in political or institutional writing
Create two versions of the same informational content for different audiences (academic vs general public) and use nominalisation as a deliberate register-shifting tool

response_modes.reason: The effects of nominalisation are best understood through contrast across registers. Students who only see nominalisation in academic texts may not grasp its ideological dimension (hidden agency) or the deliberate formality it signals. Multiple text contexts surface the range of effects.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The ideological reading of nominalisation — how it can obscure agency and create impersonality in political and institutional writing — is a genuinely rich extension that connects grammar to critical reading in powerful ways for advancing students.
success_criteria: Explains how nominalisation makes a text more formal or abstract, using a specific example from a provided text.
Discusses how nominalisation affects the relationship between writer and audience in at least one text.
